units.title: Africa since Independence
units.intro: The flag went up. The hard part started.

cards.title: 4.1 Ideals of Independence
body: The leaders of the nationalist movements at the time of independence had great hopes for their new states.
Free from foreign control, the new governments, run by Africans, would make decisions for the new nations.
The ideal of African nationalists, that Africa should decide its own destiny, seemed now to have come true.
Two of the most immediate goals of the newly independent states in Africa were promoting economic growth and ensuring national unity.
The new African leaders were optimistic that freedom from colonial control would result in economic prosperity.

cards.title: The two goals of independence, explained
body: **Goal 1 – economic growth.** The 1960s were good years: oil cost only $2 a barrel while prices of African exports (cocoa, coffee, copper) were high, so exports grew by **6 % a year**, and farming and mining expanded. Leaders believed **industrialization** was the key to breaking colonial trade patterns and dependence on the West.

**Goal 2 – national unity and African culture.** Borders drawn by Europeans ignored pre-colonial states and peoples, so leaders stressed **nation building** to unite many ethnic groups. Independence also brought a cultural revival: in **1966 Senegal** hosted the first festival of African arts and culture, and African history and archaeology became serious university subjects.
**Memory trick:** "Grow the economy, Glue the nation."
**Exam tip:** When asked about the "ideals of independence", name both goals and give one fact for each.

cards.title: 4.2 What types of states were set up?
body: Although the approaches differ from country to another, essentially states adopted either a socialist or capitalist path.
One approach to implementing the ideals of independent Africa was African socialism.
Supporters claimed that there were many indigenous aspects of socialism in traditional African societies.
Nkrumah's policy in Ghana is an example.
Agency (CIA), just nine years after coming to power as the hero of the African nationalist movement.

cards.title: State types
body: Some tried liberal constitutions, many moved to one-party or military rule “for unity”. Ideals (unity, development, dignity) collided with weak institutions.

cards.title: Nyerere's African Socialism: Ujamaa and the Arusha Declaration
body: **Step 1 – why a new model.** The fall of Nkrumah in Ghana convinced Tanzania's **Julius Nyerere** that a different kind of African socialism was needed.

**Step 2 – the Arusha Declaration (1967).** Nyerere set out the policy in the **Arusha Declaration of 1967**, based on **ujamaa** ("solidarity" or familyhood) villages. The aim was a **self-reliant** Tanzania that would depend on its own resources – mainly peasant labour – instead of foreign aid and investment.

**Step 3 – how it worked.** The state led the economy: land, large companies and banks were nationalized (with compensation), and only small firms stayed private. A **Leadership Code** banned officials from capitalist business, making Tanzania one of the least corrupt countries in Africa at the time.

**Step 4 – Nyerere's idea in his own words.** "Socialism is an attitude of mind. The basis of socialism is a belief in the oneness of man and the common historical destiny of humankind… its basis is human equality." Socialism serves people of every colour – "not the state, not the flag".
**Step 5 – the villages.** Large collective villages with communal land, shared resources and elected leaders replaced scattered farms, improving access to schools and clinics.

**Step 6 – problems.** The policy was imposed from above. Peasants did not want to leave ancestral land or private plots, so compulsory **"villagization"** was introduced (helped by the 1973–74 drought), and production suffered.
**Memory trick:** "Arusha 1967 = Ujamaa = self-reliance."

cards.problem: (Exam question) Describe the types of states set up in Africa after independence.

steps.text: Two paths: states adopted either a socialist or a capitalist path.
African socialism: supporters said traditional African society already had socialist elements – e.g. Nkrumah's Ghana.
Political systems: some began with liberal constitutions.
Drift: many moved to one-party or military rule "for unity", as high ideals met weak institutions.

cards.answer: Socialist (e.g. Nkrumah's Ghana) or capitalist states, many starting with liberal constitutions but turning into one-party or military regimes.

cards.title: 4.3 Challenges of Independence: Colonial legacies
body: Most historians agree that the colonial legacy was the underlying cause of many of these challenges.
Many historians believe that part of the explanation for this lies in the period of colonial rule, which by its very nature is oppressive and dictatorial.
The colonial authorities had kept control by using force and silencing any criticism or opposition.
After independence, many African leaders, who had themselves been prisoners of the colonial authorities, used the same methods.
By the late 1960s, many independent African countries were one-party states where opposition parties were banned and their leaders jailed.

cards.title: Colonial legacy
body: Borders that cut nations and join rivals; economies built to export one crop or mineral; few industries; schools and civil service too small; capital cities favoured over the countryside.

cards.title: Model answer: colonial legacies
cards.problem: (Exam question) Explain how the colonial legacy created challenges for independent African states.

steps.text: Political: colonial rule kept control by force and silenced criticism; after independence many leaders (often former colonial prisoners) used the same methods – by the late 1960s many were one-party states.
Borders: they cut nations and joined rivals, causing conflicts.
Economy: economies built to export one crop or mineral.
Society: schools and civil service too small, and capitals favoured over the countryside.

cards.answer: Authoritarian habits, artificial borders, one-crop export economies and too few schools and trained officials – all inherited from colonial rule – lay behind many post-independence problems.

cards.title: 4.4 Internal problems and external interventions
body: As well as the challenges resulting from colonialism, the independent African states were affected by other factors.
Others developed out of the political legacy of colonial rule, such as the impact of ethnicity, and military coups.
Two external factors which had a significant impact were the politics of the Cold War and world economic trends, which led to a debt crisis in Africa.
The climate in many parts of Africa is harsh and unpredictable.
Soil in many areas is thin and poor, resulting in low yields of crops.

cards.title: Six problems of independent Africa, one fact each
body: **1. Environment.** Poor soils and unreliable rain; the **Sahel drought of 1968–73** cut northern Nigeria's groundnut harvest from 765,000 to 250,000 tons.
**2. Population growth.** Africa's population tripled from 200 million (1950) to 600 million (2000), crowding cities.
**3. Ethnicity.** Politicians sought votes from their own ethnic groups, weakening national unity.
**4. Military coups.** More than 60 between 1963 and 1989; by the late 1980s half of Africa was under military rule (e.g. Bokassa in the Central African Republic).
**5. Debt crisis.** Oil rose from \$2 (1973 start) to \$34 a barrel (1980); in 1972 a ton of Tanzanian tea bought 60 barrels of oil, in 1980 only 4.5.
**6. The Cold War.** The superpowers armed rival sides, e.g. Soviet aid to Angola, Mozambique, Somalia and Ethiopia.
**Memory trick:** "Earth, People, Tribe, Gun, Debt, Superpowers" – four internal, two external.

cards.title: 4.5 Africa after the Cold War
body: Since 1990 most of Africa has seen political changes, as military dictatorships and one-party states have given way to multi-party systems.
A number of factors, both internal and external, have combined to bring this about.
The most important external factor was the ending of the Cold War.
Africa was no longer the playing field for influence by rival superpowers.

Corrupt and ineffective governments or long-standing dictators, such as Mobutu Sese Seko of Zaire were no longer supported with external funds or arms supplies simply because they declared themselves to be anticommunist or anti-capitalist.

cards.title: Internal + external
body: Ethnic and regional tension, coups, debt. Cold War patrons armed clients. After 1990, fewer superpower cheques, more talk of multiparty politics and structural adjustment.

cards.title: Unit 4 summary in full – Africa since independence
body: **Point 1 – different roads.** After independence African countries chose different policies: some, like **Kenya**, took a **capitalist** path; others, like **Tanzania**, followed **socialist** policies.
**Point 2 – opportunities and challenges.** Independence brought opportunities, but also many problems.
**Point 3 – ethnic conflict.** Ethnic conflicts broke out, for example the **Biafran War in Nigeria**.
**Point 4 – political instability.** It led to military coups in several states, such as **Idi Amin's coup in Uganda**.
**Point 5 – colonial economic legacy.** Colonialism left economies unbalanced and **dependent on foreign markets**.
**Point 6 – other burdens.** Drought, disease, high population growth and poverty put the new states at a disadvantage.

**Point 7 – the verdict by the end of the 1970s.** The hope that independence would bring peace and prosperity was not realized: colonial after-effects made states vulnerable to internal conflict, made worse by Cold War economic and political pressures.
**Key terms:** African socialism, capitalism, civil war, coup d'état, debt crisis, democratization, ethnicity, intervention, nation-building, neo-colonialism, Ujamaa, urbanization.
**Memory trick – "P-E-C-E-D":** Paths (capitalist/socialist), Ethnic conflict, Coups, Economy dependent, Drought and disease.

cards.title: Model answer: Africa after the Cold War
cards.problem: (Exam question) How did the end of the Cold War change African politics?

steps.text: Change: since 1990 military dictatorships and one-party states gave way to multi-party systems.
Main external cause: the end of the Cold War – Africa was no longer a superpower playing field.
Example: dictators like Mobutu of Zaire lost funds and arms they had received for being anti-communist.
Also: more talk of multiparty politics and structural adjustment, though ethnic tension, coups and debt remained.

cards.answer: With superpower support gone, dictators like Mobutu lost their backing and most of Africa moved from one-party and military rule towards multi-party systems.

glossary.meaning: Nyerere explained his version of African Socialism in the following way: Socialism is an attitude of mind.

tips.text: Once free from colonial rule, African countries pursued different polcies to construct new societies. Some, like Kenya, followed a capitalist path, while others, like Tanzania pursued socialist policies.
Independence brought opportunities and possibilities for the new states. But there were also many challenges facing them.
Ethnic conflicts broke out, such as the Biafran War in Nigeria.
Political instability led to military coups in several states, such as that of Idi Amin in Uganda.
The legacy of colonialism also left them without a balanced economy and dependent on foreign markets.
Problems such as drought, disease, high population growth rates and poverty created major difficulties as well.

The newly independent African states thus faced problems which placed them at a disadvantage in comparison to many other countries. So the hopes that independence would bring peace and prosperity to Africa were unrealized by the end of the 1970s.

The after-effects of colonialism meant that African states were particularly vulnerable to internal conflicts, and this was made worse by the impact of international economic and political factors during the Cold War.
State types: Some tried liberal constitutions, many moved to one-party or military rule “for unity”. Ideals (unity, development, dignity) collided with weak institutions.

Colonial legacy: Borders that cut nations and join rivals; economies built to export one crop or mineral; few industries; schools and civil service too small; capital cities favoured over the countryside.
Internal + external: Ethnic and regional tension, coups, debt. Cold War patrons armed clients. After 1990, fewer superpower cheques, more talk of multiparty politics and structural adjustment.
